shots.text: Right now,
you probably think people are watching you.
Judging your outfit.
Replaying that awkward thing you said yesterday.
But here's the truth...
they're not.
Psychologists call this the Spotlight Effect.

overlays.sub: WHY YOU THINK EVERYONE IS WATCHING

shots.text: In the year two thousand,
researchers at Cornell University
asked students to walk into a room full of strangers
wearing a really embarrassing T-shirt.
Afterwards, those students guessed that half the room had noticed.
The real number?
Only about twenty-three percent.
Less than one in four.
Your brain puts you at the centre of every scene,
because you are the centre of your own world.
But everyone else is doing the exact same thing.
They're too busy worrying about their own spotlight
to notice yours.
So in this video, I'll show you seven psychological tricks
to switch that spotlight off.
And we're starting with the one that almost everyone gets completely wrong.
Trick number one. Stop trying to hide your nerves.
Picture this.
You're about to give a presentation.
Your heart is pounding,
your hands are sweating,
your voice feels shaky,
and you're sure everyone in the room can see it.
It feels like your anxiety is written all over your face.
Psychologists call this the illusion of transparency.
In one study at Cornell,
people told lies
while a group of observers watched
and tried to catch them.
The liars guessed that about half of the observers would see right through them.

v.label: LIARS GUESSED THEY'D BE CAUGHT BY

shots.text: In reality, only about a quarter did.
Your inner storm is mostly invisible.
And here's the part that almost everyone gets wrong.
When we feel nervous, we try harder to hide it.
We tense up,
we avoid eye contact,
we rehearse every single word in our head.
And that actually makes us look more awkward, not less.
So the researchers tried something different.
Before a group of nervous people gave a speech,
they simply told them about the illusion of transparency.
That's it.
No breathing exercises. No pep talk.
Just the truth: your nerves are far less visible than you think.
Those speakers felt calmer,
and the audience rated their speeches as better and more composed.
So the next time your heart starts racing,
remind yourself: they can't see what I feel.
Just knowing that switches half the spotlight off.
But the next trick goes even further,
because it doesn't just calm you down.
It makes people like you more.
Trick number two. Point the spotlight outward.
Here's what happens inside an anxious brain
at a party,
a date,
or a job interview.
Your attention turns inward.
You start watching yourself like a security camera.
How do I sound?
What are my hands doing?
Is my face going red?
Did that joke land?
Psychologists who study social anxiety call this self-focused attention,
and it's the fuel that keeps the spotlight burning.
The more you watch yourself, the more awkward you feel.
And the more awkward you feel, the more you watch yourself.
It's a loop.
Imagine two people at the same party.
The first one spends the whole night thinking about how they look.
The second one spends the night
trying to find out one interesting thing about every person they meet.

The way out is surprisingly simple.
Give your attention a job somewhere else.
Get curious about the other person.
What are they really saying?
What do they care about?
What's one question you could ask that nobody else would think of?
Your brain can't fully focus on two things at once.
Every bit of attention you give to them
is attention taken away from your own spotlight.
And there's a bonus.
Researchers at Harvard found that people who ask more questions,
especially follow-up questions,
are rated as more likeable.
So the trick that calms you down
also makes you better company.
Now, what about the moments when you really do mess up?
That's where trick number three comes in.
Trick number three. Your mistakes look braver from the outside.
Imagine you have to admit you made a big mistake at work.
Or tell someone you have feelings for them.
Or ask for help when you're struggling.
In your head, it feels like weakness.
Like you're exposing every flaw you have.
But in 2018,
researchers in Germany tested exactly this.
They asked people to imagine themselves in vulnerable moments like these,
and then imagine someone else in the very same situation.
When it was them, they saw weakness and embarrassment.
When it was someone else, they saw courage, honesty, and strength.
The researchers called it the beautiful mess effect.
The same moment that feels like a mess from the inside
looks beautiful from the outside.
Think about it.
When a friend tells you they're struggling,
do you think less of them?

remember that the person watching you isn't seeing a fool.

Trick number four. They judge you less harshly than you think.
Let's say the worst actually happens.

You forget someone's name right after they told you.
You spill coffee on your shirt
just before a meeting.
Surely now, people are judging you.
Researchers at Cornell tested this too.
They had people fail at a task in front of others,

Again and again, people expected to be judged far more severely than they actually were.
Why does this happen?
Because when it's you, the blunder is the whole story.

They know you're more than one mistake,

The mistake made them seem more human.

So the next time you mess up, don't spiral.
Laugh, fix it, and move on.

Trick number five. Assume they liked you more.

researchers paired up strangers for a short conversation.

Trick number seven. Embarrass yourself on purpose.
This sounds crazy,
but it's one of the most famous exercises in therapy.

You deliberately do something mildly embarrassing in public.
